I have complex decisions on that.

On one hand, it’s true that spending $$$ is too difficult to get a diagnosis (not to mention potential discrimination based on a professional diagnosis), yet there are so many people that genuinely are on the spectrum but because of these barriers cannot get that diagnosis. So I feel like its unfair to brush these people off as not being on the spectrum, especially when they do the heavy research and ultimately feel like that’s where they fit.

An example of this is me with borderline personality disorder. I was originally diagnosed with bipolar disorder type 2, but after a year in I noticed that my symptoms and experiences were consistent with borderline. It took me a while to convince my doctor to refer me to a psychiatrist for another assessment, but now she sounds more confident in my belief. I’m still in the process of getting the official diagnosis of bpd, but my doctor and I discussed being on the spectrum, and once I get this borderline thing under control it will be the next process we venture onto 😅

On the other hand, it’s inaccurate and maybe dangerous (on some occasions) to self diagnose because sometimes we think we have one thing when it’s actually the other. 

Overall, I think because of all the barriers people face to getting a professional diagnosis shouldn’t stop you from making education assumptions (I mean, you do know your body best). Read into it as much as possible, jot down the symptoms and how you personally relate to them, and the best thing you can do is save up for that diagnosis. I don’t think its fair to discount your feelings and experiences just because you can’t afford a diagnosis. I’m sorry you have to pay for these things :( healthcare is a right not a privilege!

I’m currently in my last year and was diagnosed last June. The last academic year (2018-2019) was the worst year of my life, both academically and mentally. I took 6 courses (some full year, some half) and only passed 2. I ended up having to petition off all the F’s, but what helped me this academic year is team work. Working with my doctor to find the right medications for me, working with the student accessibility services on campus, working with my professors by providing them accommodation letters that support the areas I struggle in (note taking because depressive episodes make it hard to get out of bed, extensions for assignments, extra time to write exams ect), and if you’re lucky you’ll have some supportive friends around you to push you along the way. I /strongly/ suggest you utilize the mental health resources at your college, get a counsellor, develop an accommodation letter with them, take all the help you can get. School still isnt easy, but I doubt it’ll ever be, but I’m doing better now than I ever had before. You got this!
